idiom_name: Laminar + Waypoint router: currentPageSignal selects the view, split keeps it alive
implementation_notes: In Scala the realistic realization is a reactive router: Waypoint's Router[Page] owns which view is current (currentPageSignal) and Laminar/Airstream renders it with child <-- views, where views is a Signal[HtmlElement] produced by splitMatchOne or SplitRender - the split key keeps the element for a page alive across updates so only the data inside it changes, which is the 'one owner switches and syncs the views' contract without a class hierarchy. The registry half is the route table plus the current-page signal, and per-view state lives in the view's own Vars. Airstream ownership is the part to get right: subscriptions created outside an implicit Owner are not cleaned up automatically, so dynamically created views must be created under the page's (or the split's) owner or they keep observing the model after the page is gone; the retained-controller style is not worth reproducing in Scala.
code_sketch:
val router = new Router[Page](routes, getPageTitle = _.title,
  serializePage = p => Json.encode(p).toUtf8String,
  deserializePage = s => Json.decodeString(s).to[Page].value,
  routeFallback = _ => NotFoundPage)

// one signal decides which view exists; splitMatchOne avoids re-creating it on switch
val views: Signal[HtmlElement] = router.currentPageSignal.splitMatchOne
  .handleValue(HomePage)(HomeView())
  .handleType[DashboardPage] { (initial, pageSignal) => DashboardView(pageSignal) }
  .toSignal

val app: Div = div(h1("Shell"), child <-- views)   // handler owns switching + syncing
router.pushState(DashboardPage(...))                // switch; data flows through the signals
pitfalls: Airstream subscriptions need an Owner: elements created outside split/splitOption (or without an owner) are not cleaned up and keep observing the model after the view is gone.

Rendering a Signal[HtmlElement] with child <-- recreates the element on every emission; use split, splitMatchOne or SplitRender to keep the element and update only its data, or every switch tears down and rebuilds the subtree and its state.
splitMatchOne/handleType match on the runtime type (ClassTag), so page case classes with type parameters do not discriminate reliably.
The router stores the current page in browser history, so state that is not serializable into the page value is lost on reload - keep it in the view's own Vars instead of in the page case class.
